questions.q: Which is the correct order of authority at any intersection (highest first)?
a: Emergency vehicle → officer/lights → signs & markings → tram → right-before-left
questions.e: Read every intersection top-down: a live emergency vehicle beats everything, an officer or working light beats the signs, signs and paint beat the default, the tram gets its place, and only a truly bare crossing falls back to right-before-left.

questions.q: At an unmarked equal crossing, a car from the LEFT arrives well before you do. Who goes first?
a: The car from the left — it arrived first
You — right-before-left, arrival time is irrelevant
questions.e: Right-before-left is not first-come-first-served: the car on the left yields to you regardless of who arrived first.

questions.q: You face this give-way sign. The crossing road is completely empty. Must you stop?
a: No — yield only; stopping is needed only if traffic comes
questions.e: B6 requires giving way, not stopping. On an empty road you may continue — unlike the stop sign, which demands a full stop every time.

questions.q: You and an oncoming car both go straight ahead through an equal intersection. Who goes first?
a: Neither yields to the other — you pass each other normally
questions.e: Two vehicles going straight from opposite directions don't cross paths — no priority question arises between them. Priority rules bite only where paths cross.

questions.q: Shark's teeth point at YOUR lane at a cycle crossing on a roundabout exit. A cyclist approaches on the crossing. What do you do?
a: Wave the cyclist through only if they stop
questions.e: Shark's teeth on your lane always mean you yield — here to the cyclists on the crossing. Paint carries the same authority as a sign.

questions.q: A fire engine with blue lights and siren approaches while you wait at a red light. What is the correct action?
a: Drive through the red light immediately
Make room safely — without blindly running the red
Stay exactly where you are, always
questions.e: You must let it pass, but 'make way' never means blindly jumping a red into cross-traffic. Move aside where it is safe and possible.

questions.q: An unmarked equal crossing: a moped approaches from your right on the road. Who goes first?
a: You — mopeds always yield to cars
The moped — right-before-left counts for all drivers
questions.e: Right-before-left applies to all drivers — mopeds and cyclists included. From the right, the moped goes first.

questions.q: You drive on a priority road (yellow diamond). Does right-before-left apply at its crossings?
a: No — crossing traffic yields to the priority road
questions.e: On a priority road the sign, not the default, decides: crossing traffic gives way to you. Right-before-left only rules truly equal, unmarked crossings.

questions.q: Which shape/colour is a WARNING?
questions.e: Red triangle warns, red circle forbids, blue circle commands, blue square informs — the four-shape system that replaces memorising a catalogue.

questions.q: What is the difference between this empty red ring and the red disc with a white bar (no entry)?
a: This closes the road in BOTH directions; the white-bar disc closes it from one side
This one applies only to trucks
questions.e: C1 (empty ring) = closed to all traffic in both directions. C2 (white bar) = no entry from your side — usually a one-way street's exit.

questions.q: What does this blue circle with circular arrows command?
a: Follow the roundabout in the direction of the arrows
questions.e: A blue circle commands: this is the mandatory direction around the roundabout. (Priority at the entries is set separately, by the shark's teeth.)

questions.q: If the exam offers 'you must stop' or 'you must give way' as the meaning of this sign, what should you answer?
a: Neither — a triangle only warns; the answer is 'be alert'
questions.e: A red triangle never requires an action. 'Must stop' and 'must give way' next to a warning sign are planted traps — the answer is awareness.

questions.q: What does this triangle with a tram warn of — and what should you already know about trams?
a: Tram crossing ahead — and at equal crossings the tram goes first
questions.e: The triangle warns of a tram crossing. Pair it with the rule: at equal crossings the tram has priority from any direction.

questions.q: To which shape/colour family does a speed-limit sign belong?
a: Information — it just shows a number
Prohibition — the red circle forbids going faster
questions.e: The red ring makes it a prohibition: it forbids exceeding the number. That is why exceeding it is an offence, unlike the blue advisory square.

questions.q: Solid and dashed centre lines lie side by side, the SOLID one nearest your lane. May you overtake across them?
a: Yes — the dashed line allows it
No — you obey the line on your side, and yours is solid
questions.e: You read the line nearest you: solid on your side means no crossing, whatever lies beyond it.

questions.q: What does a blue circle with a white bicycle (G11) mean for a cyclist?
a: They MUST use this cycle path
questions.e: Blue circle = command. For cyclists the path is compulsory; for drivers it means that lane is off-limits to cars.

questions.q: You are on the autosnelweg at 08:00 on a workday. Entry signs said 130. Your maximum now?
questions.e: 08:00 falls inside the 06:00–19:00 window: the daytime cap of 100 applies on every Dutch motorway, whatever the entry signs promised for the night.

questions.q: At night on the motorway, where no signs allow more, what is the limit?
a: The signed limit for that stretch — 130 only where signed
questions.e: 130 at night applies only where the signs say so; some stretches stay at 100 or 120 around the clock. The signs on your stretch decide.

questions.q: INSIDE the built-up area you pass this end-of-50 sign. What is the limit after it?
questions.e: The end sign returns you to the road-type default. Inside the built-up area that default is 50 — so here the sign changes nothing in practice.

questions.q: What makes a ZONE speed sign different from an ordinary speed sign?
a: It covers a whole area, unrepeated, until the end-zone sign
questions.e: An ordinary sign governs the road it stands on; a zone sign governs every street inside the area until the grey end-of-zone sign.

questions.q: In the erf, roughly what does 'walking pace' (stapvoets) mean in practice?
questions.e: The legal standard is walking pace; in practice that is taken as roughly 15 km/h. The exam answer to 'how fast in the erf' is: walking pace.

questions.q: A numbered speed sign is nowhere to be seen, but you just passed a town-name sign. The limit is…
questions.e: The town-name sign IS the speed rule: entering the bebouwde kom sets the 50 default without any number being shown.

questions.q: Road type says 130 (night motorway), the matrix shows 100, your caravan caps you at 90. What do you drive?
questions.e: Three limits can apply at once: road, sign, vehicle. The rule that resolves it is absolute — the lowest number wins.

questions.q: Who enforces the number on this blue square?
a: Nobody — it is advice (adviessnelheid), not a limit
questions.e: Blue square = information: the advisory speed. Exceeding it is not an offence in itself — but the road's real limit and the duty to drive safely still apply.

questions.q: You approach roadworks where a temporary 70 sign stands on a motorway stretch normally allowing 100. You drive 85. Offence?
a: Yes — the temporary sign is the current limit
questions.e: A posted (including temporary) sign overrides the default: 70 is the limit until it ends. The lowest applicable number always governs.

questions.q: Before every right turn in the Netherlands, what extra check is essential?
a: Mirror and shoulder check for cyclists coming up on your right
questions.e: Cyclists going straight beat your right turn, and they approach in exactly the spot mirrors miss. Mirror, shoulder, cycle path — then turn.

questions.q: Must the rider of a yellow-plate bromfiets wear a helmet?
questions.e: Bromfiets riders have always been required to wear a helmet. Since 2025, snorfiets riders must too.

questions.q: A pedestrian stands at the zebra, clearly about to step onto it. You are close. What must you do?
a: Continue — they have not stepped out yet
Be able to stop and give way — 'clearly about to cross' already counts
questions.e: Zebra priority starts when someone is visibly about to cross, not when they are in front of your bumper. Approach every zebra at a speed that lets you stop.

questions.q: What is the 'mirror test' for driving near a truck?
a: If you cannot see the driver in his mirror, he cannot see you
questions.e: The test is symmetric visibility: no eye contact via his mirror means you are in the dode hoek. Position yourself where his mirrors can find you.

questions.q: The bus pull-out rule — giving a signalling bus the chance to leave its stop — applies where?
questions.e: The rule applies inside the built-up area: a bus signalling to leave its stop must be given the opportunity there.

questions.q: What single principle organises the Dutch rules about other road users?
a: The more fragile the road user, the more the rules protect them
Whoever pays more road tax goes first
questions.e: Pedestrians and cyclists get the strongest protection; you in the car carry the responsibility — and next to a truck, the fragile one is you.

questions.q: How do you tell a snorfiets from a bromfiets at a glance?
a: Number-plate colour: blue = snorfiets, yellow = bromfiets
questions.e: The plate is the whole answer: blue = snorfiets (25, cycle path), yellow = bromfiets (45, road in town).

questions.q: May you STOP (not park) on a marked cycle lane to quickly drop off a passenger?
a: No — on a cycle lane both stopping and parking are forbidden
questions.e: The stopping-versus-parking distinction does not help you here: a marked cycle lane belongs to the bikes, and you may neither park nor stop on it.

questions.q: A driver with a 3-year-old licence blows 0.3 promille. Legal?
a: No — the novice limit of 0.2 applies for the first five years
questions.e: Three years into the licence the novice limit (0.2) still applies — 0.3 is over it. The same value would be legal for a ten-year licence holder.

questions.q: You have parked at the kerb, engine off, and pick up your phone. Offence?
a: Yes — you are in the car
No — parked with the engine off, you are no longer driving
Only if the key is in reach
questions.e: The ban binds drivers, and parked out of traffic you are no longer one. In moving or waiting traffic — including red lights — holding the phone is the offence.

questions.q: Are seatbelts required in the BACK seats?
questions.e: Belts are for everyone, every seat, every trip — no back-seat exception, no short-trip exception.

questions.q: A police officer asks to see your licence during a routine check. What is the rule?
a: You must carry it and show it on demand
questions.e: The rijbewijs must be carried while driving and shown to police on demand — one of the four paperwork conditions of a legal drive.

questions.q: How do the police test for drug use at the roadside?
questions.e: Since 2017 roadside drug checks use a saliva test, with zero-tolerance limits — any measurable amount of illegal drugs is an offence.

questions.q: With some yellow-sticker medicines, what can the pharmacist tell you about driving?
a: Driving is always fine after one hour
With certain medicines you may not drive at all
questions.e: The sticker means 'find out' — and for some medicines the answer is a genuine driving ban. 'The doctor prescribed it, so driving is fine' is the trap.

questions.q: Your passenger is 11 years old and 1.50 m tall. What is required?
a: The normal seatbelt — height decides, and 1.50 m is above the line
questions.e: The line is 1.35 m: taller children wear the normal belt. (You as driver remain responsible for belting passengers under 12.)

questions.q: What does this sign mean?
questions.e: The greyed, struck-through zone sign ends the parkeerschijfzone — beyond it, disc rules no longer apply.

questions.q: You arrive in a blue zone at 14:05. What time do you set on the parking disc?
a: 14:30 — arrival rounded UP to the next half hour
questions.e: The disc is set to your arrival time rounded up to the next half hour — here 14:30 — and laid visibly on the dashboard.

questions.q: May you park at a marked bus stop?
a: No — a bus stop is an automatic no-parking place
questions.e: The bus stop is in the family of automatic, unsigned bans — like the 5-metre rules, driveways, cycle lanes and the pavement.

questions.q: Why does the law require 1.6 mm of tyre tread?
a: Tread channels water away — below it, grip in rain collapses
questions.e: Tread depth is about wet grip: the grooves evacuate water. Below 1.6 mm the tyre is illegal and genuinely dangerous in rain.

questions.q: What is the danger of using the rear fog light in ordinary rain?
a: It dazzles the driver behind and masks your brake lights
questions.e: That piercing red lamp blinds the driver behind you and drowns out your brake lights — which is why it is only legal below 50 m visibility.

questions.q: Which costs you extra fuel at motorway speed?
a: An empty, unused roof box left mounted
questions.e: Drag eats fuel: an empty roof box left on the car costs real consumption at speed. Take it off when unused.

questions.q: What is a milieuzone?
a: A nature reserve you may not drive through
A city area that excludes the most polluting (usually older diesel) vehicles
A zone where the engine must be off
questions.e: Some city centres are environmental zones excluding the oldest diesels; the boundary sign says which vehicles may enter.

questions.q: Daytime motorway, the car ahead does 90 and you want to pass. May you 'briefly' do 120 to overtake quickly?
a: Yes — brief overtaking speed is allowed
No — there is no overtaking exception to a speed limit
questions.e: Limits cap the manoeuvre, not the other way round. If 100 is not enough to overtake safely, the answer is: don't overtake.

questions.q: On the exam, two answers both seem defensible. Which should you pick?
a: The first one you thought of
The more careful, anticipating one — usually reducing speed or increasing distance
questions.e: The exam has a consistent personality: the defensive, anticipating option wins. Speed writes the cheque for every mistake — in doubt, slow down or make space.

questions.q: What is the core skill behind every insight question?
a: Anticipating what COULD happen — hidden and vulnerable road users acting
questions.e: Insight questions are never about what is happening — they are about what could. Identify who is hidden or fragile, assume they act, and have your response already chosen.
